# **Architectural Overhaul of Neuromorphic Counter-UAS Perception: Ego-Motion Compensation and Minimal-Latency Pipelines on Edge AI Hardware**

## **Introduction and Problem Statement**

The deployment of neuromorphic event-based vision for Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS) offers unprecedented advantages in high-dynamic-range target acquisition and microsecond-level temporal resolution. Conventional frame-based cameras suffer from motion blur and dynamic range limitations when attempting to resolve small, fast-moving drone propellers against bright skies or dark foliage. Event cameras, by contrast, asynchronously measure per-pixel logarithmic illuminance changes, delivering an extremely sparse, high-fidelity data stream that perfectly captures the high-frequency micro-flicker of rotating blades1. However, transitioning event-based sensors from static tripod mounts to mobile or panning platforms introduces severe algorithmic and hardware bottlenecks.  
In this analysis, the specific failure modes of an event-based drone detection pipeline—utilizing a Sony IMX636 event sensor coupled with a Bosch BHI260AP Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB—are thoroughly deconstructed. The primary symptoms observed by system operators include an approximate 4-to-5 second processing delay in the event camera pipeline when the camera is static and the drone is moved, alongside catastrophic target lock failure when the camera and coupled IMU are subjected to ego-motion4.  
This report evaluates whether the Jetson Orin Nano 8GB is underpowered for this specific use case, conducts a comprehensive review of publicly available research and open-source code for event-based ego-motion compensation, and establishes the optimal, minimal-latency perception pipeline. By transitioning from sequential CPU event handling to batched GPU acceleration (CUDA/cuFFT), implementing ![][image1] micro-neighborhood periodicity sieves, locking IMU/sensor clock epochs, and dynamically warping anticipatory neural masks, the end-to-end processing latency can be reduced to sub-millisecond realms while preserving the structural integrity of the drone's aerodynamic signature4.

## **Edge AI Hardware Evaluation: The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB**

A fundamental question surrounding the observed 4-to-5 second processing delay is whether the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB possesses sufficient computational bandwidth to process high-resolution event streams (capable of reaching 10 to 40 million events per second) in real-time.

### **Compute and Memory Bandwidth Specifications**

The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB represents a massive generational leap over previous embedded hardware platforms. At its core, the architecture features an NVIDIA Ampere GPU equipped with 1024 CUDA cores and 32 Tensor Cores, delivering up to 40 Trillion Operations Per Second (TOPS) of AI inference in standard configurations, and up to 67 TOPS in the Super Developer Kit variant7. This GPU is supported by a 6-core Arm Cortex-A78AE CPU running between 1.5 GHz and 2.0 GHz, depending on the specific module iteration7.  
Crucially for event-based vision, which relies heavily on asynchronous memory access rather than dense matrix multiplication, the 8GB 128-bit LPDDR5 memory subsystem delivers a unified memory bandwidth of 68 GB/s (and up to 102 GB/s in updated hardware revisions)8. This unified memory architecture allows both the Arm CPU and the Ampere GPU to access the same memory space directly, minimizing the data transfer bottlenecks that typically plague traditional computing architectures when handling continuous, high-throughput asynchronous data streams6.

| Hardware Metric | Jetson Nano (Legacy) | Jetson Orin Nano 8GB | Generational Multiplier |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **GPU Architecture** | Maxwell (128 Cores) | Ampere (1024 Cores \+ 32 Tensor Cores) | ![][image2] Core Count |
| **AI Performance** | 0.47 TOPS | 40 to 67 TOPS | ![][image3] to ![][image4] Increase |
| **CPU Architecture** | Quad-core Arm A57 | 6-core Arm Cortex-A78AE | ![][image5] Cores, ![][image6] IPC |
| **Memory Bandwidth** | 25.6 GB/s | 68 GB/s to 102 GB/s | ![][image7] to ![][image8] Increase |
| **Camera Interfaces** | 2x MIPI CSI-2 | Up to 4x MIPI CSI-2 (8 lanes total) | ![][image9] Bandwidth Capacity |

### **Diagnosing the 4-to-5 Second Bottleneck**

Given the specifications outlined in the comparative data, the Orin Nano 8GB is demonstrably overpowering for standard neuromorphic processing. The observed multi-second latency is not a symptom of insufficient silicon, but of a software architecture falling into a classic Von Neumann bottleneck4.  
When the event camera is observing a static scene, it generates a resting rate of 200,000 to 500,000 events per second. However, during ego-motion—such as panning the camera across textured backgrounds like foliage or structural edges—the asynchronous pixels trigger en masse, spiking the data ingestion rate to between 4.3 and 14 million events per second (MEv/s)5.  
In the initial pipeline architecture described in the system logs, the CPU callback thread ingested this event stream and performed per-event spatial operations. Specifically, the software executed pthread\_mutex\_lock acquisitions on every single event to update spatial patch grids and evaluate neural suppression masks6. At 10 MEv/s, this generated an astounding 20,000,000 mutex lock attempts per second, driving a single Arm Cortex-A78AE core to 146% utilization through severe thread contention5.  
Simultaneously, the pipeline attempted to compute 512-point sliding NDFT/FFT arrays sequentially on the CPU across 80+ active spatial cells. This caused computational spikes of 35 to 45 milliseconds per frame cycle5. Combined with unoptimized browser MJPEG network buffering over persistent HTTP/1.1 TCP connections without socket bounding, the Linux TCP stack queued dozens of frames in memory5.  
The transition from this sequential CPU processing methodology to a batched GPU execution framework utilizing CUDA and cuFFT eliminates this bottleneck entirely. The performance differential between the legacy software architecture and the hardware-optimized architecture proves that the Orin Nano is highly capable.

| Performance Metric | Legacy CPU-Bound Pipeline | Optimized GPU-Accelerated Pipeline | Hardware Impact |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **End-to-End Latency** | 1,500 ms to 2,000 ms | \< 25 ms | Achieves hard real-time tracking constraints |
| **Mutex Locks per Second** | 20,000,000 | 0 (Lock-free atomic double-buffering) | Eliminates thread contention |
| **FFT Compute Time (1152 cells)** | 35 ms to 45 ms | 0.34 ms | ![][image10] speedup via batched cuFFT execution |
| **CPU Core Utilization** | 146% (Backpressuring ring buffers) | 82% (Stable with massive headroom) | Frees CPU for higher-level tracking logic |

The data unequivocally indicates that the 4-to-5 second delay is a software routing issue. By offloading spatial array updates and Fourier transforms to the 1024 Ampere CUDA cores, the Jetson Orin Nano easily achieves sub-25 millisecond real-time performance5.

## **Theoretical Foundations of Event-Based Vision and Propeller Signatures**

To design an optimal ego-motion compensation pipeline, it is necessary to rigorously define the mathematical signatures of drone propellers versus background ego-motion clutter within an asynchronous event stream.

### **The Continuous-Time Event Generation Model**

Unlike standard frame-based cameras that integrate photons over a fixed exposure time to produce synchronous matrices of absolute intensity, event cameras feature independent pixels that respond asynchronously to changes in logarithmic illuminance. An event ![][image11] is triggered when the contrast change at a specific coordinate exceeds a pre-configured hardware threshold ![][image12]1. The generative event model is defined as:  
![][image13]  
Under camera motion characterized by an optical flow vector ![][image14], the linearized event generation equation becomes dependent on the spatial gradient ![][image15] of the scene13. By replacing the right-hand term with a first-order approximation, the event generation rate induced by ego-motion is:  
![][image16]  
This implies that when an event camera is rotated, any static background texture with a high spatial gradient (such as building edges or tree branches) will generate a massive wave of events proportional to the angular velocity of the camera13.

### **The Propeller Micro-Flicker Harmonic Signature**

In stark contrast to the aperiodic edges generated by background motion, a drone propeller modulates the scene's brightness as the physical blades periodically occlude and reveal the background illumination. At a specific pixel observing the rotor, the resulting event stream can be modeled as a non-uniform sampling of an underlying periodic rectangular wave2.  
For a given blade-pass frequency ![][image17], a period ![][image18], and a duty cycle ![][image19] representing the fraction of the period the pixel is occluded, the idealized occlusion signal ![][image20] is expressed as a pulse train2:  
![][image21]  
Because this signal is continuous and ![][image22]\-periodic, it admits a Fourier series expansion. The power spectrum ![][image23] of this signal consists of distinct impulse spikes (a harmonic comb) at integer multiples of the fundamental blade-pass frequency2:  
![][image24]  
This harmonic comb—typically manifesting between 80 Hz and 800 Hz depending on the drone's aerodynamic profile and RPM—provides a highly distinctive, physics-grounded fingerprint. This signature allows perception systems to discriminate UAV pixels from background motion, windblown foliage turbulence, and other non-periodic environmental clutter2.

## **State-of-the-Art in Event-Based Drone Detection and Ego-Motion**

Addressing the challenge of detecting micro-flicker during ego-motion requires synthesizing current academic literature and available open-source implementations. The research landscape provides several complementary approaches to robust drone tracking.

### **Frequency-Domain Analysis and HelixTrack**

Traditional frame-based object detectors absorb massive per-frame label budgets during training and struggle to generalize to the micro-second domain. Methods like the one proposed by Bezick and Sahin in *Real-Time Drone Detection in Event Cameras via Per-Pixel Frequency Analysis* utilize purely analytic, frequency-domain techniques (such as the Non-uniform Discrete Fourier Transform, NDFT) to identify the harmonic comb structure2.  
Further advancing this is *HelixTrack* (CVPR 2026), an open-source, fully event-driven framework designed for tracking and measuring spinning propeller-like objects (available at github.com/radimspetlik/helixtrack)16. HelixTrack turns the adversarial motion pattern of a propeller into a trackable feature. Incoming events are back-warped from the image plane into the rotor plane via a homography17. The system utilizes a continuous-time acceleration prior and a Kalman filter to update the phase of the rotor on a per-event basis, rendering the tracker invariant to arbitrary in-plane camera rotations17. HelixTrack effectively demonstrates that maintaining microsecond latency and continuous-time tracking is superior to batching events into pseudo-frames.

### **EventRadar and Synthetic Aperture Scanning**

The *EventRadar* system illustrates the extreme long-range capabilities of event sensors. While standard RGB methods fail at 300 meters, EventRadar achieves high mean Average Precision (mAP) by focusing on dense, periodic event footprints18. To reconcile the narrow field of view required for long-range optics with the need for wide-area surveillance, EventRadar employs a scanning strategy inspired by Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)18. The event camera is mounted on a 2-Degree-of-Freedom (DoF) gimbal integrated with an IMU. During rapid scanning, events are ego-motion compensated and reprojected onto a global spherical frame18. This proves that with precise IMU synchronization, continuous rotational motion can be completely mathematically negated.

### **Anticipatory Neural Motion Suppression**

While frequency domain isolation is powerful, deep learning approaches offer robust macro-level segmentation. *EVPropNet* demonstrated the efficacy of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on synthetic propeller data for dynamic dodging and pursuit2. More recently, the Robotics and Perception Group at the University of Zurich (UZH-RPG) published *Motion-aware Event Suppression for Event Cameras* (RSS 2026), providing an open-source implementation (github.com/uzh-rpg/event\_suppression)21.  
This UZH-RPG framework introduces an anticipatory masking technique. Standard neural segmentation suffers from latency; applying a computed mask ![][image25] from time ![][image26] to the current event stream results in spatial misalignment for moving objects6. The UZH-RPG method employs a recurrent encoder-decoder with Attention-based Time Conditioning (ATC) to predict future optical flow. By propagating the segmentation mask forward in time, the system anticipates and suppresses events corresponding to the static background with zero effective latency5.

### **Continuous-Time Contrast Maximization**

For environments lacking a tightly coupled IMU, continuous-time ego-motion compensation can be achieved purely visually through Contrast Maximization. Pioneered by Gallego et al., this unifying framework warps spatio-temporal volumes of events to maximize the sharpness (variance) of the resulting aggregated image3. The framework models the continuous dynamics of the camera using spline trajectories or Gaussian Process regression, enabling accurate 6-DoF motion compensation25. However, when an IMU is available—as is the case with the Bosch BHI260AP—direct rotational integration is computationally cheaper and highly deterministic.

## **Root Cause Analysis of Ego-Motion Tracking Failures**

Despite the theoretical availability of these techniques, the specific implementation running on the Jetson Orin Nano failed catastrophically when moved. The immediate loss of the detection boundary on the drone propeller was traced to a confluence of coordinate unwarping errors, temporal history fragmentation, and physical optical limitations.

### **Clock Synchronization Phase Lag and Homography Failure**

Continuous-time ego-motion compensation relies on projecting incoming events back to a stable reference frame. Under pure rotational camera motion characterized by the angular velocity vector ![][image27], an event ![][image28] is unwarped to a reference epoch ![][image29] via spherical homography5:  
![][image30]  
Where ![][image31] is the camera intrinsic matrix, and the rotation matrix ![][image32] is the exponential map of the integrated angular rates6.  
The primary cause of the tracking failure was a severe epoch mismatch in the software stack. The Metavision OpenEB event timestamps operated on a microsecond uptime clock (e.g., ![][image33] since boot), while the serial reader for the Bosch BHI260AP IMU logged data using the host system's standard epoch clock (e.g., ![][image34])5. When the homography warper queried the IMU buffer using the camera's timestamp, it searched billions of microseconds in the past. Consequently, the binary search clamped to the very first static sample at boot, returning an Identity Matrix (![][image35]) for every event5.  
In effect, absolutely zero ego-motion stabilization was occurring. The pipeline was running entirely uncompensated on the raw sensor plane.  
Without stabilization, a camera panning at a moderate ![][image36] causes a physically static drone to sweep across approximately 92 pixels on the sensor over a 128-millisecond window5. Because the frequency-domain detection engine relies on a 128 ms (512-sample) sliding FFT window housed in fixed spatial grid cells, the drone's periodic signal was shattered across three or four separate spatial cells5. The coherent integration time within any single cell collapsed, dropping the fundamental peak power into the Poisson noise floor, resulting in an immediate loss of the tracking boundary5.  
![][image37]

### **The F/8 Optical Clutter Phenomenon and Sub-Pixel Jitter**

Beyond clock synchronization, the choice of an Edmund Optics 8mm ![][image38] M12 lens (\#27052) was a critical physical contributor to the erratic tracking behavior. The ![][image38] aperture features a minute physical opening (![][image39] clear aperture), which produces an extreme hyperfocal depth of field5. While beneficial in traditional photography, this is highly detrimental to event cameras under ego-motion for two critical reasons:

> 1. **Pseudoperiodicity from Spatial Texture Scanning:** With everything from 1.5 meters to infinity in razor-sharp focus, distant foliage and rooflines present high-contrast optical edges. When the event camera pans across periodic spatial textures (e.g., leaves with a spatial spacing ![][image40]) at a scan velocity ![][image41], it generates an apparent temporal frequency: ![][image42]5. Panning at ![][image43] generated artificial temporal harmonics around 172 Hz, directly overlapping with genuine drone blade passage frequencies5.  
> 2. **Photoreceptor Bandwidth Deprivation:** The event camera's logarithmic front-end has an intensity-dependent temporal cutoff frequency. An ![][image38] lens admits ![][image2] less light than a standard ![][image44] lens. Under low photon flux, the pixel analog response slows, increasing event timestamp latency (![][image45]) and expanding timestamp jitter from an ideal ![][image46] to ![][image47]5. This temporal blurring degrades the microsecond phase coherence required for strict periodicity sieving.

To resolve these optical limitations, replacing the lens with a wider aperture configuration is mandatory.

| Lens Model (Commonlands) | Focal Length | Aperture (F\#) | Optical Resolution | Photon Gain (vs f/8) | Optimal Application Profile |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **CIL083** | 8.0 mm | ![][image44] | 8 MP | ![][image48] | Direct drop-in replacement. Preserves 44.5° HFOV while eliminating photoreceptor lag. |
| **CIL078** | 7.8 mm | ![][image49] | 8 MP | ![][image50] | Best for high-speed tracking in low-light environments. |
| **CIL122** | 12.0 mm | ![][image49] | 12 MP | ![][image50] | Extended range (100ft+). Provides 1.5x optical magnification for distant rotor resolving. |

Switching to an ![][image44] lens focused at the hyperfocal distance naturally introduces slight optical low-pass Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) rolloff on close foreground foliage, heavily attenuating the high-frequency clutter event generation while providing the necessary photon flux for microsecond timing accuracy5.

## **The Optimal Minimal-Latency Processing Pipeline**

To synthesize a solution that entirely bypasses the limitations of sequential CPU processing, the architecture on the Jetson Orin Nano must be restructured into a highly parallelized, asynchronous pipeline. The optimal solution is a four-tier hybrid ego-motion compensation framework that heavily leverages the Ampere GPU ecosystem.

### **Tier 1: Continuous Gyroscope Spherical Homography (Hardware Stabilization)**

The foundational layer is continuous mathematical stabilization. The Arduino Nicla Sense ME (Bosch BHI260AP) must be rigidly mounted directly to the camera chassis. Because drones are engaged at standoff ranges (![][image51]), scene depth is massively larger than the physical baseline offset between the IMU and lens (![][image52]), rendering parallax errors negligible5.  
To solve the clock phase lag, a continuous microsecond clock offset anchor must be established on the very first incoming packet:  
![][image53]  
This is subsequently filtered via an exponential moving average to ensure the host-to-camera time conversion maintains zero phase lag5.  
To eliminate the CPU bottleneck of per-event matrix inversions, homography must be applied as a fast batch transformation. Over a 1 ms event batch (approximately ![][image54]), angular velocity is functionally constant. The homography matrix ![][image55] is computed once. Every event coordinate is then transformed using 8 scalar operations without a single mutex lock5:  
![][image56]

### **Tier 2: Micro-Neighborhood Periodicity Sieve (Asynchronous Harmonic Gating)**

As noted in the *HelixTrack* research, rigid single-pixel filtering fails at long ranges because atmospheric turbulence and hand tremor cause sub-pixel spatial jitter17. A drone blade might trigger pixel ![][image57] on one revolution and ![][image58] on the next.  
The optimal filtering approach is a Surface of Active Events (SAE) Micro-Neighborhood Periodicity Sieve. By maintaining a ![][image59] pixel tile memory layout, the algorithm evaluates the inter-event interval ![][image60] across neighboring pixels5.

* If ![][image61], the event matches a physical rotor frequency (![][image62] to ![][image63]) and is retained5.  
* Single-shot ego-motion edges (which pass over the pixel once and leave it silent) yield ![][image64] and are discarded in ![][image1] time5.

By executing this sieve directly on the GPU in CUDA Unified Memory (cudaMallocManaged), the pipeline drops 98% of aperiodic background events before they ever reach the FFT grid, reducing data throughput during fast pans from ![][image65] to ![][image66] in under 5 nanoseconds per event5.  
![][image67]

### **Tier 3: GPU-Accelerated Batched cuFFT Engine**

Once events are stabilized and filtered, they are binned into a spatial grid operating at 4000 Hz temporal resolution to support Fourier extraction. Previously, computing these FFTs sequentially on the Arm Cortex CPU took up to 45 ms. The optimal minimal-latency solution leverages the Jetson Orin Nano's 1024 Ampere CUDA cores. By utilizing batched 1D Fast Fourier Transforms (cufftExecR2C), the hardware can process all 1152 spatial channels (576 base cells and 576 pooled cells) concurrently in parallel5. This parallelization reduces the steady-state spectral analysis latency from 35 ms down to an imperceptible 0.34 ms5.  
To counter false alarms caused by extreme-value thermal shot noise in dark conditions, the peak detection logic must dynamically adapt. A Median CFAR (Constant False Alarm Rate) estimator is required to calculate the wideband noise floor:  
![][image68]  
This method cleanly rejects low-frequency foliage turbulence that would otherwise elevate an arithmetic mean, securing a pristine ![][image69] SNR under dynamic ![][image36] camera panning5.

### **Tier 4: Anticipatory Neural Motion Suppression**

For macro-level background suppression and visual odometry telemetry generation, the pipeline integrates the UZH RSS 2026 Anticipatory Motion Suppression architecture (ConvGRU \+ Attention Time Conditioning)5.  
Because neural network inference inherently takes time (measured at 14.01 ms on TensorRT FP16)5, applying a calculated mask ![][image25] to the current real-time event stream results in spatial mismatch due to target displacement during the compute window. The optimal solution incorporates backward flow warping. The network forecasts the future optical flow ![][image70], projecting the dynamic Independently Moving Object (IMO) mask forward5:  
![][image71]  
This zero-latency event masking operates via an asynchronous gating operator6. To execute this without choking the OpenEB USB ingestion thread, the TensorRT engine must output its results to a ping-pong double buffer swapped via lock-free atomic pointers (std::atomic\<const float\*\>)5. By completely eliminating CPU mutex contention, this multi-threaded design prevents buffer overruns and contributes to lowering the total end-to-end pipeline latency to under 25 milliseconds5.

## **Advanced Sensor Fusion: Optical Cross Section (OCS) and Active SPAD Illumination**

While the event camera serves as a highly robust, 100% passive, and covert early warning tripwire, relying on 2D angular data alone limits the system's ability to determine the absolute physical scale of the target. A small DJI quadcopter at 20 meters exhibits identical angular dimensions to a massive heavy-lift agricultural drone at 150 meters. To move from detection to definitive physical classification, the event camera must seamlessly hand off target coordinates to an active 1D Direct Time-of-Flight (dToF) Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) or Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM)5.

### **The Disaggregated Hardware Reality**

Tactically and physically, it is impossible to mount a high-power active SPAD and pulsed laser system on a dismounted warfighter's helmet. The optical collection aperture required to capture single photons returning from 100 to 300 meters mandates a 30 to 50 mm glass lens5. When combined with the necessary high-voltage bias boost (![][image72]), thermal Peltier cooling elements to suppress dark counts (15W-35W), and the destabilizing torque of biomechanical neck jitter, head-mounting is rendered unviable5.  
The disaggregated architecture is therefore the sole optimal path. The event camera, drawing ![][image73] and weighing just 45 grams, operates as the wearable Tier 1 tripwire5. Upon detecting a continuous harmonic comb, the Orin Nano calculates the precise optical ray vector ![][image74] in degrees of Azimuth and Elevation and broadcasts this cue over a low-latency tactical mesh network. The Tier 2 heavy vehicle, automated weapon station, or tripod-mounted system then autonomously slews a coaxial SPAD receiver and pulsed Near-Infrared (NIR) laser strictly to that exact bearing5.

### **Absolute Optical Cross Section and Z-Axis Pulse Stretching**

Once cued, the 1D SPAD transceiver flood-illuminates the narrow target window with a sub-nanosecond NIR laser pulse. The returning Time-of-Flight (![][image75]) provides the absolute range ![][image76]. This precise ranging unlocks two vital physical classification measurements5:

> 1. **Absolute OCS Normalization:** The Event Camera's pipeline receives the range data and normalizes the total returning photon count (![][image77]) against the inverse-square geometric drop-off (![][image78]) to calculate the true reflective surface area of the drone: ![][image79]5. This reliably separates lightweight commercial drones from heavy-lift tactical variants.  
> 2. **Z-Axis Pulse Stretching:** When a drone flies at an oblique angle relative to the sensor, photons reflecting off the front rotors will return fractions of a nanosecond earlier than those reflecting off the chassis and rear rotors. Utilizing a high-speed Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) with 20-picosecond resolution, the returning 1D temporal histogram spreads into multiple distinct peaks. The time delay between these peaks (![][image80]) yields the exact physical front-to-back wheelbase length of the airframe in inches5.

It is critical to note that investing in expensive 2D scientific SPAD arrays (such as the SPAD23 at \$20,000 to \$35,000) or pursuing proprietary automotive LiDAR silicon is a costly architectural misstep for this specific use case5. Commercial automotive LiDARs pre-process data directly into 3D point clouds on the silicon, entirely discarding the raw picosecond temporal histograms required for sub-inch pulse stretching5. The optimal, cost-effective field deployment path pairs a standard C-mount Single-Photon Counting Module (SPCM, e.g., the MPD PDM-C or Thorlabs SPDMA) with a dedicated USB Time-Tagger to stream raw 20-picosecond TCSPC histograms directly into the Jetson Orin Nano for fusion with the passive event stream5.

## **Conclusion and Recommendations**

The inability to retain detection boundaries during ego-motion and the multi-second processing delays on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB were not hardware deficiencies. The Orin Nano is an exceptionally capable edge computing platform. The failures were the direct result of applying synchronous, sequential, frame-based programming paradigms to an asynchronous, multi-megahertz neuromorphic data stream.  
To achieve continuous, reliable target lock under dynamic ego-motion, the architecture has been entirely restructured. The optimal processing pipeline demands the following strategic implementations:  
First, an immediate optical retrofit is required. Replacing the ![][image38] lens with an ![][image44] or ![][image49] M12 lens (such as the Commonlands CIL083) will boost incident photon flux by ![][image2], slash photodiode analog latency, and optically filter distant high-frequency spatial clutter through depth-of-field blurring5.  
Second, precise clock synchronization must be hardcoded. Implementing a continuous microsecond clock offset anchor ensures that the IMU host timestamps and the OpenEB camera timestamps align perfectly, permitting the ![][image81] homography matrix to unwarp events with zero phase error5.  
Finally, the software pipeline must fully transition to the GPU. Eliminating all per-event CPU mutex locks and routing the event stream through a GPU-based Micro-Neighborhood Periodicity Sieve allows the system to discard aperiodic background edges in ![][image1] time. Followed by batched cuFFT analysis across all spatial cells, this unified CUDA pipeline reduces total system latency to under 25 milliseconds, achieving robust target lock at panning speeds exceeding ![][image36] while leaving ample CPU headroom for tactical telemetry distribution5.
